video_title: Lawfare Daily: The Rise of the Military-Technology Complex with Bernice Yeung
transcript: It's the LawFare podcast. I'm Tyler McBryan, managing editor of Lawfair with Bernice Jur, the managing editor at UC Berkeley School of Journalism's Investigative Reporting Program. Today, we're talking about Bernice's recent feature, [music] the rise of the military technology complex, published in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. We discussed the bumpy history of big tech's relationship with US [music] defense contracting, how Silicon Valley has reshaped the Pentagon, and how in turn the Pentagon has reshaped Silicon Valley. So, Bernice, I'm really excited to talk to you about this story. It's so rich in detail. There's so much great history there, but it also speaks so much to our current moment. So, just to get everyone on the same page, I would love it if you could lay out the story uh as you see it, the story that you tried to tell uh and then we will most certainly drill down on on a lot of these chapters. >> Well, first of all, thanks so much for having me on the podcast. I'm a big fan of lawfare um someone who's really interested in how the legal system works and policy. So, thanks for having me. Um so the story really um you know started out with um my trying to understand the relationship between Silicon Valley and the Pentagon and how um that relationship has changed over time. I grew up um in the Silicon Valley and in in kind of the 80s9s uh time period I was in San Francisco during the dotcom boom and bust. And of course, we're all familiar with the Silicon Valley's deep um defense roots, the the funding and the um collaboration uh with defense and tech um you know leading to its very um creation um and foundations. But there was that period of time where there seemed to be less emphasis, less presence um overt presence of the Pentagon in Silicon Valley. Um, and then all of a sudden, fast forward some, you know, decades later, and, um, I was looking, I was just thinking about that, um, kind of indelible image of all of the tech CEOs standing behind um, you know, in the, you know, at the White House inauguration, Trump's inauguration. And it was really that question of like, how did we how did we get here um, all of a sudden? And so, um, this story was really an effort to kind of unpack, um, what's been going on in in recent decades that led to kind of this, uh, at first a kind of almost uncoupling divorce between Silicon Valley and the Pentagon and how they've come back together. >> Yeah, thank you for that. And you mentioned that a lot of us do know of course how intertwined the histories of Silicon Valley/ the US tech sector are with the Pentagon histories of DARPA and the birth of the internet. But as you lay out so well a lot of people have also forgotten that uh history. Um, so I actually would love to start with the where you start Silicon Valley's uh story in the the history of Silicon Valley and and how it was actually shaped as you said by defense uh spending and funding. Um I think it's a helpful place to start because I I get the sense that in in popular discourse there is this idea that Silicon Valley was born in the '90s with the dot uh boom etc. But as you know and as you lived it started much sooner. So, um, if we could actually start there and then I'm I do want to move to the the Last Supper, um, cuz that was a great place that you started your piece. Well, um, you know, going back to the the 50s and and roundabout there, you know, if you think about the term Silicon Valley, it comes from companies that were making Silicon semiconductors for the defense department at a point in time when uh, nobody else could really afford Silicon, you know, these foundational components of computers, these at that time these enormous machines that would take up entire rooms. only the government could really afford um you know these these um significant and expensive um and very powerful um computers. And so um it was really you know that defense spending and that um investment in Silicon Valley technology by the defense department that enabled computing and then the internet and then uh you know Siri and self-driving cars and all of all all of that. But I think there has been, you know, for the popular imagination, Silicon Valley is often associated with consumer technology, with, you know, apps, with social media, with um all of, you know, B2B technology because that was a huge emphasis for several decades as Silicon Valley began to realize that there was significant funding available through the global consumer market, uh that there were ready-made customers there and that there was simultaneously um it was harder uh to sometimes do business with the Pentagon. There's lots of regulations, lots of laws, um lots of process. And so there I think that was kind of what started to lead to this uh separation. They were just kind of off doing their own thing for a period of time. I'm not saying that um you know there was a complete separation between Silicon Valley and the federal government. I mean at the same time Silicon Valley was becoming this kind of global center of of capital and became a global industry and it was quite present in uh in terms of lobbying in terms of seeking regulation or deregulation that would suit them um different policies that would be favorable to them. So there was involvement with the federal government, but in terms of defense and this and Silicon Valley um there was just this kind of cooling period for several decades. And then there's of course um cultural splits. DC and Silicon Valley are very very different places. I mean it's almost too easy to caricature the two, you know. Um, I mean, I've I've read some of the books by some of the defense tech uh leaders and and one theme that comes up a lot is how the folks from Silicon Valley are always showing up at these DC meetings, you know, in hoodies and then the DC guys are coming to the Silicon Valley meetings and suits and everybody's just kind of, you know, looking past each other culturally, too. >> And timelines are on, you know, one is moving in eons and the other one is moving in seconds. And I I really liked that you started your piece with this this I I hesitate to call it uh history because there is an element of of self mythology as well, but this episode of the Last Supper. This is not only a story that that that you're telling, but it's also a story that Silicon Valley is telling itself right now. Um so could you unravel that tale a bit? >> Yes. The Last Supper. Um it is it is a tale. I think it is a narrative. It's it's a bit of mythology. I mean, it it's based in obviously something that actually happened, which is essentially in the early 90s as kind of the cold war was was starting to wind down. There was a sense that we were going to go into a kind of peace dividend uh period where less spending was going to be directed towards um you know, defense. And so the assistant secretary of defense at the time summoned all of the defense contractors in the country. At that time there were dozens in the in the realm of you know 50 or so. Not all of them but he summoned some of them to the White House. Um and I'm sorry to the Pentagon. And um they had this dinner that was called the Last Supper. And apparently you know this invitation was quite mysterious. People didn't exactly know why they were being asked to go. after the meal they were ushered into this kind of uh you know meeting space where they were told you know I think the according to the mythology that they needed to consolidate or die because the defense dollars were just going to plummet in the years coming and it wasn't going to be something temporary it was going to be something long-term and everybody needed to kind of plan accordingly um I I should point out that there have been some critiques of that analysis is like kind of the the beginning point of all of the consolidation that happens. Kind of this notion that because of it there's um there's been no innovation or little innovation at the Pentagon. I think, you know, it was arguably a factor, but there have been some really great um analysis by folks like Margaret Mullins um at Vanderbilt uh policy accelerator who who digs into that and and points to kind of a longer history of uh kind of privatization and um disinvestment in um in kind of federal policy and spending that that have led to that have kind of also helped usher in the consolidation of these defense contractors now down from dozens to you know the big five. Um so yeah it was you know it's really viewed as this pivotal moment and certainly um it's it's captures a lot of our imaginations in terms of how we got here but um uh it's it's also I think arguably more complicated than just that one dinner leading to where we are today. So right, so this this episode that uh part history, part mythology uh in the fall of 1993 of the consolidation of the these contractors in um Silicon Valley turning toward the consumer now that we have the end of history and the peace dividends. Your point is absolutely right. you know it is too tidy of a narrative and it's uh it's um it's a bit convenient but in broad strokes a as you've also written there were larger dynamics of uh innovation happening more so in the the private consumer markets and Silicon Valley you know making apps etc. Meanwhile the Pentagon growing more bloated and uh not not moving very quickly and uh and relying on you know the same contractors uh in general. you had a great uh pull quote from Alex Karp's book and I'm not um in the habit these days of quoting Alex Karp much but I thought his his point was a good one from his book the technological republic he writes quote a generation of founders cloaked themselves in the rhetoric of lofty and ambitious purpose merely to build photosharing apps and chat interfaces for the modern consumer so you know in broadstrokes these dynamics were happening so it's it's easy then to understand I think you know why the Pentagon needed Silicon Valley, but what I really appreciated from your piece is how it happened. Um, you get into some of these mechanisms and, you know, structurally why it's happening. Could you speak about some of those? So, starting at our our too tidy of a starting point in the fall of 1993, how did we get here um to where we are today when Trump uh at at the inauguration there are all these tech CEOs and founders, you know, kind of paying their respects and this revolving door happening. How did we get here? Well, I do think that, you know, beginning with folks like Peter Theal, Alex Karp, Palmer Lucky, these are some of the, you know, founders, co-founders of what you might call now kind of the defense tech, you know, uh, pioneers, uh, who, you know, Palanteer started in the early 2000s. um Anderil, another one started uh you know in about 2017 or so and they just took a very different point of view which is that they believed that technology needed to be returned to kind of thinking about the so-called national project um and doing work for the national interest. I think there had become, you know, a a disdain almost that had developed between DC and the Pentagon for a period. Um just a real misunderstanding and not a lot of conversation. I mean, Mark Andre of um, you know, the big venture capitalist in a podcast talks about how he felt like, you know, DC hated Silicon Valley for a period of time and that kind of the you know, the feelings were were were fraught between them. I think because of this culture difference where there was a deep skepticism from some uh corners of Silicon Valley around government work, especially defense work, lots of skepticism around wars, skepticism around privacy and surveillance. you know, I think Edward Snowden and what happened in that episode where it was discovered that the US government was, you know, essentially uh spying on its citizens and and um hacking into, you know, tech company in in order to do it was was really uh created a split and so there was a lot to overcome. But yes, as you say, the Pentagon was, you know, has long realized that it needs Silicon Valley. It needs the technology it's developing and it has long realized and has been part of developing AI for example, but figuring out how to get it into um weapon systems and you know battlefield management and intelligence you know analysis uh programs has been the big question mark. So they've been trying to figure out how to incorporate all of these technologies that have been developing so quickly in kind of the private and consumer uh markets. And what they did was, you know, they made a very concerted effort round about 2015 through something called unit X or the um defense innovation unit experiment. There was a very explicit effort by the defense secretary at the time, Ash Carter to go to Silicon Valley, went directly to Stanford University to give a talk and where he announced uh the creation of DIUX, which would, you know, as he promised, would help Silicon Valley and and the Pentagon do deals together, figure out how to get rid of some of the red tape that was really slowing things down. Because I think that's a really important piece of it is that you know part of part of the reason that Silicon Valley had kind of turned away from uh Pentagon business was it was just taking too long. It it was uh ponderous process and lots of bureaucracy and Silicon Valley just culturally doesn't have and practically doesn't have um the patience for it. So, so with this kind of announcement of DIUX that was kind of this big kind of lobby u first volley um to saying you know we welcome Silicon Valley back to the Pentagon and we would like to figure out how to move faster. We want to recognize you as a valuable partner and we will do what we can to um make it possible for us to work together again. >> And did that work? I mean, I asked that a bit flippantly, I guess. Um, because, you know, in in my mind, it took a few years, I think, for the the two cultures to feel each other out. Um, you know, now it's it's more common place to hear an Alex Karp talk in these um like civilization saving terms that are very uh high-minded but in, you know, motivating a a more closeness between the Pentagon and Silicon Valley. But I think, you know, around that same time, 2016, there was um around that time or shortly after Mark Zuckerberg being dragged in front of Congress and there's still a lot of um contention uh between the the two coasts. So, how so how did that um process play out in the ensuing years after that announcement? >> I think the big game changer here is really the promise of of money and funding. Um there's, you know, obviously a nearly trillion dollar budget that the Pentagon is operating with, perhaps soon, far more than that. um as the as two of the early leaders of DIUX put it in their book, you know, there may have been skeptics in the audience, but um and I'm quoting here, um the skeptics in the audience might not have been moved by the stuff about defending the Western liberal order, but they did care about money. Carter's message was loud and clear. The Pentagon was open for business and wanted to push a giant shopping cart down the aisles of Silicon Valley. So I think they, you know, Silicon Valley for its part saw a business opportunity and a really potentially lucrative one and a really stable one. >> Uh, and then of of course the a downside of that is that money can create all sorts of incentives, not all of them good or truthful. So, one thing I was really curious about asking you about is um a bit of a a quick side note here of a few years ago, I believe in 2022, I interviewed a journalist named Jonathan Guyire about a story he wrote for Vox about a new exciting defense tech startup called Rebellion Defense. Uh and and in Jonathan's reporting, he made the argument that they weren't quite um they they were essentially selling um you know, a false bill of goods. They were often slapping AI or artificial intelligence onto products without actually having the technology to back it up. a bit of a um an Elizabeth Holmes uh type of situation because of the huge windfall that was promised uh by by this influx of of spending, defense spending into the tech sector. As you point out, I think and it's very important to say that a lot of these newer companies uh investments in AI are sort of a drop in the bucket compared to these traditional weapons manufacturers and defense contractors. the Loheed Martins are still accounting for the lion share of a lot of these massive uh defense funding numbers. But, you know, I'm curious how you were able to to how you made sense of the sometimes unreliable narrators who are these founders who uh have a very strong financial incentive to make their tech sound good and sound like it works. I think the the moment where I realized um how hazy um gray or illdefined um AI and its capabilities are came to me pretty early on the in the reporting when I was simply trying to understand how much money um the Pentagon was spending on unclassified AI related projects. I look at that now and I see it as such a fool's errand. But of course I didn't know that at the time. I was just looking at kind of the contracts that have been awarded related to artificial intelligence. And then of course soon you realize, you know, there are 16 million different ways to describe artificial intelligence. Large language models, you know, um, aentic AI. I mean, there's all a bazillion different keywords you could potentially use. And some of some of those terms are not even used in AI related projects. There was uh you know companies with AI in the name where it's not clear what exactly they were doing for the government. And I think there is this you know there's a frothiness around AI that is attracting a lot of excitement um in some circles a lot of anxiety among others and I think the the the hardest thing initially was to figure out what what do we mean by AI in this context and um you know the Pentagon like other federal departments and agencies is using AI in really kind of mundane ways and the way that maybe all of us use AI um you know for to to review HR you know job applications for example or uh things of that sort. I think you know it became clear that what we wanted to focus on was the deployment of artificial intelligence for the purposes of warfare. Um and so we started to focus in on those types of kind of frontier AI companies that were getting hundreds of thousands of uh defense dollars explicitly for um you know autonomy uh things like uh you know computer vision things where there you're automating um analysis and and um supporting the deployment of weapons. But I think it is, as you're saying, um, a really big black box as to what is AI. And I think it's it's illdefined. And I think that's part of it being this emerging technology, but also part of what makes it in, you know, really scary in certain senses, um, and uncertain. Um, and it makes it hard to know whether we're getting uh a good deal as taxpayers. And it's also making it hard, you know, to know whether um we're deploying those technologies in an ethical and responsible way. >> Your your piece is largely a history of how Silicon Valley and and the Defense Department came back together or, I don't know, fell back in love. But so many points of your piece stuck out to me of the limitations that still exist between this relationship, these inherent cultural legal mismatches. Um, one of them that comes to mind immediately is often um two two things that are often in tension which is innovation and regulation or innovation and safety. This is a constant uh conversation especially with regard to AI and autonomous. Um, I can't remember exactly who you quoted in in the piece, but you know, if it was up to a lot of the the Silicon Valley leaders, uh, we would really throw the guardrails off so that America could have the the best chance it has at developing the most lethal weapons, strongest defense. But I think to to the Pentagon's credit, a lot of people in the military would be apprehensive to to to throw those off or move too quickly. So, I'm curious, you know, what your thoughts are on on the limitations that still like what are the limits of how close Silicon Valley and the Pentagon can get? Yeah. I don't know. whether that's a good thing or a bad thing. >> I think that, you know, I've I've spoken to some um folks who have worked um in kind of the defense apparatus, you know, in in the government um and under different administrations. And I think they they feel that because this is when we're talking about using AI and warfare uh that because it is life and death uh and because it's not just the life and death of civilians, it's also life and death of the so-called war fighter. There's a lot of caution that will be required in testing and um making sure that things are working as promised. Um that's that I think is their expectation. I think that what what what's different now and I don't know how it's going to play out is that um Silicon Valley is now much more involved and making a much more concerted effort um in terms of lobbying in terms of making donations to say the House and Senate Armed Services Committees to seek the policies and and uh you know approaches that suit them. You know, I I looked at, you know, lobbying expenditures and and and campaign contributions and those numbers are are just, you know, on the on the on the rise for these defense tech companies and tech companies. So, I think the real question is as Silicon Valley's voice is is louder and more likely to be heard, um, is there going to be a counterveailing force that's really advocating simultaneously for, you know, deploying all of these technologies in a safe, strategic, um, ethical and responsible Um, and I think what's what we're actually starting to see, it's always so interesting is what's happening on on kind of the, you know, AI, uh, worker front. Um, they have been some of the most vocal in terms of voicing their concerns around doing work with the Pentagon in a way that they didn't feel there were enough ethical guidelines. thinking of Google during the project maven period. Uh but also some of the open AI employees have recently you know donated significant sums to a pack called um guardrails alliance that seeks to uh increase regulation around how AI is used. So I think it's just you know Silicon Valley is a formidable formidable you know industry and and voice and I think it's about you know we'll have to see if there are entities or uh communities that are are going to have a significant um kind of counterveailing um argument. Yeah, I'm glad you brought that up because it reminds me of what I thought when I read that Alex Karp quote, which again I agree with the observation that the in the the social media era that founders would often sell their products in these worldsaving rhetoric when in reality it was often like a photo app that they were building. But the conclusion that he draws from that is different from what I would draw that and therefore they should live up to these uh lofty ideals by building defense tech when you could see the same starting point end up with building you know new and innovative ways to tackle climate change or medicine or uh curing cancer etc. Not to say that a lot of Silicon Valley companies are are looking at these other existential risks and and more global issues, but clearly the big players are are are have coalesed around the idea of of you know building things for for the Pentagon and for the US military. I'm curious yeah what the the the tech worker uh movements are an interesting one. I'm curious if you if you do see other counternarratives or other um other places that Silicon Valley is going or is this this movement toward the Defense Department so widespread now? It's just kind of it's it's the the norm in Silicon Valley. >> I I think that it's a really rapidly growing sector. Um there's a organization called the Silicon Valley Defense Group that um is made up of um you know folks from DC and folks out here in Silicon Valley and they issue a report every year looking at kind of venture capital spending and and you know their most recent report which came out in the spring of last year says that uh this you know this this has really been a banner year for defense tech investment by venture capital. Uh so I think that's a really strong indication that you know people who are trying to uh seek significant returns from their investment are see are betting on the Pentagon essentially or companies that are going to do deals with the Pentagon. So I don't think that you know genies going back in the bottle necessarily. I think we're just going to see probably more of it. And I think our job um as uh journalists and as uh members of the public is to to ask the government to be really um you know sensible in how it's deploying its financial resources toward um toward this industry uh in the way that we would with any other government spending. I think because AI is just such a black box um and it's as we were talking about illdefined it it merits more scrutiny because we need to make sure that um we're we're getting you know what we're paying for as tax as taxpayers and I think we're also in a moment where uh I think we have an administration that is very eager to um accelerate AI adoption that is uh seeks deregulation um and then simultaneously is not um particularly transparent and has been um uh quite uh combative in terms of um even answering basic questions from reporters. So that I I do think that there's a sense of urgency um in this moment as as defense tech is rising and lots of money is pouring into that sector that we really uh kind of keep our eyes and ears open for what's actually happening with our money. I think a lot of our listeners are are more familiar with how Silicon Valley has been changing DC and the beltway, but given that that you're from Silicon Valley and I believe you're based in um Berkeley or the Bay Area um generally, I would love to hear from just from your observations dayto-day how you have seen or not DC/ the Pentagon changing Silicon Valley. I I don't know things like the ads that you see on the BART or things like that. I don't know if it is the vibe different. How have you seen, you know, your uh hometown changing because of this relationship? >> You know what's really interesting is um the article that I wrote I sent out to um you know folks I grew up with again here in Silicon Valley whose parents worked for Silicon Valley startups or for IBM. Um my dad worked for IBM and various startups and they didn't know some of this history um which I found fascinating. You go to the computer history museum um in in the peninsula and you don't really see this kind of uh laid out e you know as as as directly. And so I think we're all kind of just waking up in the same way that, you know, we saw that picture of all the tech executives at uh the Trump inauguration and everyone, you know, was surprised. I think we're we're we're still, you know, working our way through and wrapping our mind around how the industry is in fact changing. Um, I think that there is, if you look for it, uh, some obvious clues that that all of this is on the on the uptick. If you go on to YouTube or, you know, anywhere, you can you can listen to hours upon hours uh of defense tech podcasts um all of all of the um leaders of uh these defense tech companies um opining on various things all the time. I think also what I don't have a clear picture on is is I I'm um perhap um almost stereotypically I'm at UC Berkeley but you know Stanford is the place that has been a big incubator of a lot of these ideas. It's where you know Theel and Karp and others and have have emerged from and so that I imagine if if I were sitting there I I would see it um much more overtly the changes and I think probably I would have noticed it sooner. >> And as we uh near the close here I'm just curious to hear if you'll be continuing along this beat if you have uh any follow-up stories in mind. Um what's what's next for your reporting interests along this topic? >> Yeah, thanks. I mean, I've been trying to figure out a way to to really delve into Silicon Valley, the place, you know, that I feel um shaped a lot of who I am um and um how I approach journalism. So um I've been thinking a lot about uh a component of the reporting uh that uh emerged from this story which is kind of looking at something called other transactions which I think people you know in defense circles probably um in DC are you know have heard of have some familiarity with but they're a type of mechanism for um essentially doing a deal with a government entity that has this authority and the Pentagon is one of them that strips away a lot of the bureaucracy and red tape. And so that's obviously very appealing to um industries like Silicon Valley, defense tech, but as one expert told me um it's also a really great way to seed corruption and and other um problematic um approaches to obtaining government money. And so I'd like to just understand a little bit more how this um how this mechanism this vehicle is used do a bit more of a kind of thorough accounting of um those transactions um because I don't think there's a lot of transparency around them and they are at the moment the preferred vehicle for um buying defense tech software and technology. >> Well, that sounds even more in the weeds and therefore even more of a lawfare topic. Um, so we'll definitely have to have you back uh if you're up for it. But the article, I encourage everyone to read it. We will be linking it in the show notes. It's called uh the rise of the military technology complex. It's in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. Britney, thank you so much for joining me today. Thank you so much for having
